title: Bleach Bypass
description: Bleach bypass retains silver during processing, or simulates that retention, so the dye image sits on leftover metallic density. Contrast rises, grain shows, saturation falls, and highlights turn harsh rather than candy-colored.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: The world looks abrasive, contaminated, or exhausted. Combat, crime, and unforgiving cities live here because color has been punished, not tastefully split.
Skin can go towards brass or grey. Blacks pack down.
It is a coordinated tonal system, not just the removal of hue. It is the wrong tool when you wanted complementary studio punch.

Teal and Orange keeps faces warm and skies cyan; bleach-bypass does not throw a party on the color wheel. It is also the wrong tool if you need full Monochrome: there is still some chroma, just crushed.
A simple Desaturation without the silver contrast is a paler, softer cousin.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: For a digital recreation, grade contrast, saturation, and highlight roll-off separately and test skin. Lift nothing in the blacks that should stay packed.
Keep a little hue so it does not collapse into black and white unless that is the intent. Original films may use different negative, intermediate, or print treatments; do not assume one lab recipe.
Prompt: Bleach-bypass look on [Subject], retained silver, crushed color, harsh contrast, metallic midtones.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it for war, crime, or a world without mercy: a landing, a hunt through rain, a fluorescent interrogation. Do not use it as a synonym for teal-orange action gloss, and do not call every desaturated image bleach-bypass.

blocks.text: Desaturation only pulls chroma; contrast and silver behavior may stay gentle. Monochrome removes hue entirely.
Teal and Orange is a complementary grade with warm skin. Tonal Contrast is how you place dark against light in the rectangle, not a lab process.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Saving Private Ryan's combat imagery has a harsh, desaturated, high-contrast character associated with silver retention. Se7en packs interiors and city scenes with dense shadows and restrained color.
Minority Report is often cited for a related cold, dense, drained finish. Grammar of density, not a still to clone.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Name silver, crush, and metal. Bleach-bypass look on [Subject], retained silver, crushed color, harsh contrast, metallic midtones.
Add grain if the stock would show it. Do not write teal-orange, and do not ask for candy complementary skies.

Rain-soaked industrial street with restrained color, dense but separated blacks, pale stressed skin and hard wet highlights. Bleach-bypass-inspired tonal treatment, visible fine texture, no crushed black voids or monochrome conversion. Slow observational camera.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Teal and Orange or mild Desaturation. The tell is warm peach skin against cyan night, or a flat grey wash with no extra density.
Fix: packed blacks, harsh highlights, drained but not absent color, metallic mids. A look label does not verify the exact photochemical stage of a particular release.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is bleach bypass in film?
It is a silver-retention process, or a digital imitation, that leaves metallic density in the image. Contrast and grain go up, saturation goes down, and highlights look harsh.
Bleach Bypass vs Desaturation
Desaturation only reduces chroma. Bleach bypass also densifies the image: deeper blacks, harsher highlights, a metallic leftover. Drained color without that density is not bleach-bypass.
When should I use bleach bypass?
Use it for war, crime, or any world that should feel merciless and abrasive. Skip it for studio complementary gloss and for true black and white.
How do I prompt bleach bypass for AI image or video?
Write: Bleach-bypass look on [Subject], retained silver, crushed color, harsh contrast, metallic midtones. Forbid teal-orange skin splits and candy saturation.
